motion: Is Christianity more reasonable than atheism?

bridges.description: Christianity is more reasonable if its account of God, reason, morality, suffering and history explains the evidence better than the atheistic alternatives considered.
The specifically Christian conclusion depends on historical warrant for Jesus, especially the resurrection, rather than generic theism alone.
Christianity gains comparative support if it supplies coherent grounds for rational inquiry, moral value, meaning and hope.
Atheism is more reasonable if evidence against a perfectly good God and against distinctive Christian claims outweighs Christianity's proposed explanations.
The amount and severity of apparently preventable suffering count as probabilistic evidence against an omnipotent, omniscient and perfectly good deity.
Christianity is less reasonable if its historical, scriptural or moral claims conflict with evidence or defensible moral principles.

sections.title: Comparative standards and worldview scope
sections.rationale: The motion requires standards for reasonable belief, a precise definition of atheism, distinct burdens for atheism and Christianity, and awareness that the two do not exhaust all worldviews.

sections.title: Evil, freedom and final justice
sections.rationale: Tooley's central evidential case concerns preventable suffering; the replies address moral grounding, limits on harmful freedom, finality of judgment and promised justice.

sections.title: Science and rational inquiry
sections.rationale: The exchange distinguishes scientific compatibility, mechanism and agency, rational reliability, empirical testing of Christianity and evidence for common descent.

sections.title: Ultimate explanation and complexity
sections.rationale: Audience discussion isolates whether ultimate reality may be eternal, whether explanatory simplicity favors naturalistic histories, and whether information supports agency.

sections.title: Biblical history and reliability
sections.rationale: The speakers dispute historical interventions, composite-source arguments, scriptural genre and the reliability of miracle testimony.

sections.title: Prophecy and supernatural evidence
sections.rationale: A sustained exchange tests alleged return predictions and competing interpretations, while audience answers qualify the evidential status of possession reports.

sections.title: Morality, atonement and meaning
sections.rationale: The debate addresses objective value, Christian moral doctrines, substitutionary atonement, divine participation in suffering, forgiveness and ultimate meaning.

moves.speaker: John Lennox
moves.claim: Faith should be assessed by asking what it is placed in and what evidence supports it, rather than being treated as necessarily blind.
moves.warrant: Lennox says faith is present in science, philosophy and Christianity and contrasts evidence-based faith with blind faith.
moves.inference: If Christian faith is answerable to evidence, its reasonableness can be compared on evidential rather than definitional grounds.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This compact closing portion of Lennox's opening states the evidential standard and its contrast with blind faith.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: What is the evidence for what you believe?
Is it evidence-based faith or is it, as Richard Dawkins says, blind faith?
moves.attributionRationale: This is within Lennox's uninterrupted opening turn ending at event 201.
moves.importanceRationale: It establishes Lennox's standard for the comparative motion but does not itself supply the Christian evidence.

burdenContact.rationale: It frames Christianity as an evidence-assessable position.

moves.speaker: Michael Tooley
moves.claim: The diversity and incompatibility of religions, together with the close relation between belief and parental inheritance, make critical comparison necessary.
moves.warrant: At most one incompatible religion can be true or closest to truth, while most believers inherit beliefs associated with their parents.
moves.inference: Without serious examination of alternatives including atheism, inherited religious belief is unlikely to be epistemically justified.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This complete argument begins with why religious reasonableness matters and ends after the prescribed practice of engaging thoughtful disagreement.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: only one at most can be the one true religion
subject those beliefs to careful close uh critical scrutiny
moves.attributionRationale: This lies in Tooley's uninterrupted opening turn.
moves.importanceRationale: It supplies a comparative epistemic challenge relevant to Christianity without by itself establishing atheism.

burdenContact.rationale: It places Christianity among alternatives requiring comparative justification.

moves.speaker: John Lennox
moves.claim: Christianity rests on the historical claim that God became human in Jesus, whose life, miracles, death and resurrection provide evidence, and offers forgiveness as a gift rather than earned merit.
moves.warrant: Lennox identifies Jesus' divine-human identity, salvation from sin, resurrection as historical fact with substantial evidence, and forgiveness received through repentance.
moves.inference: If these historical claims are warranted, they provide specifically Christian reason to accept the worldview and its account of reconciliation with God.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span contains the full transition from Christian revelation in history through Lennox's stated evidence base and the distinctive forgiveness claim.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: death and resurrection from the dead
based not on merit or performance
moves.attributionRationale: The moderator explicitly hands the question to Lennox, whose answer is uninterrupted here.
moves.importanceRationale: This is Lennox's central specifically Christian constructive case.

burdenContact.rationale: It identifies the historical evidence that must bridge generic theism to Christianity.

moves.speaker: Michael Tooley
moves.claim: Atheism, as Tooley uses the term, denies an omnipotent, omniscient and morally perfect person rather than every possible deity.
moves.warrant: He defines theism minimally by those three attributes and distinguishes it from a creator that lacks perfect goodness.
moves.inference: His later evil argument targets the Christian-type perfect God without purporting to disprove deism or every supernatural being.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This span contains Tooley's complete stipulated definitions and ends before he begins giving his reason for atheism.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: Atheism is the view that uh there is no such person
moves.attributionRationale: The moderator asks Tooley to define atheism and his answer is clearly owned.
moves.importanceRationale: It fixes the target and limits of Tooley's adopted burden.

burdenContact.rationale: It specifies which God-concept Tooley's atheism denies.

moves.speaker: Michael Tooley
moves.claim: Horrendous natural and moral evils are probabilistic evidence against an omnipotent, omniscient and perfectly good deity.
moves.warrant: Tooley uses preventable typhoon deaths and human atrocities as cases a sufficiently powerful good being could prevent, and explicitly describes the argument as evidential.
moves.inference: The observed quantity and severity of apparently preventable suffering reduce the probability of the Christian God.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span starts when Tooley begins his typhoon example and ends with his explicit evidential conclusion, excluding the preceding definition of atheism and deism.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: why wouldn't he intervene in this sort of situation
that's evidence against the existence of God
moves.attributionRationale: The moderator names Tooley and the ensuing answer is uninterrupted.
moves.importanceRationale: Tooley repeatedly identifies evidential evil as his principal argument for atheism.

burdenContact.rationale: It states the probabilistic bridge from suffering to atheism.

moves.speaker: John Lennox
moves.claim: Atheism does not remove suffering, removes ultimate hope of compensation, and appears to undermine the objective moral categories used to call suffering evil.
moves.warrant: Lennox argues that suffering remains under atheism, cites the absence of afterlife compensation, and invokes Dawkins's description of a universe without good or evil.
moves.inference: The problem of evil does not straightforwardly favor atheism if atheism neither remedies suffering nor grounds the moral outrage central to the objection.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span begins when Lennox turns from his human-suffering preface to the actual comparative argument: atheism leaves suffering in place, removes ultimate compensation, and raises a moral-grounding challenge.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: you haven't removed the suffering it's still there
where does the concept of evil come from?
moves.attributionRationale: Lennox begins after the moderator's invitation and explicitly addresses Michael.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly contests both the comparative benefit and moral premise of Tooley's central argument.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues Christianity better accommodates moral judgment and ultimate hope.

responseComponents.description: Challenges whether atheism can use objective evil as evidence while lacking ultimate hope or moral grounding.

moves.speaker: Michael Tooley
moves.claim: Atheism does not entail the absence of objective morality, immaterial minds or an afterlife.
moves.warrant: Tooley points to atheist moral realists and ethical intuitionism, and distinguishes his own skepticism about an afterlife from atheism as such by citing atheist belief in reincarnation.
moves.inference: Lennox's claims that atheism removes morality and all postmortem hope assign atheism commitments it need not have.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This passage contains Tooley's complete two-part clarification concerning moral realism and afterlife beliefs among atheists.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: there are a number of philosophers uh who are moral realist
it's possible to be an atheist and have a different view
moves.attributionRationale: The moderator invites Tooley's response, and the turn is uninterrupted.
moves.importanceRationale: It corrects central burden assignments about what atheism entails.

burdenContact.rationale: It prevents the comparative case from treating atheism as identical to materialism or denial of afterlife.

responseComponents.description: Rejects the claimed entailments from atheism to moral nihilism and no afterlife.

moves.speaker: Michael Tooley
moves.claim: Christian doctrines of condemnation and hell may present a bleaker outcome for sufferers than atheistic final death.
moves.warrant: Tooley contrasts finite suffering followed by death with the possibility, under his stated reading of Christianity, that many victims face eternal punishment.
moves.inference: An afterlife does not automatically give Christianity an advantage in hope or moral consolation.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This span begins with Tooley's direct comparative question and includes the complete Holocaust-survivor illustration needed for his comparative consolation claim.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the alternative is eternal punishment and hell
is that a brighter picture?

moves.importanceRationale: It directly tests Lennox's hope argument while depending on a disputed doctrinal reading.

burdenContact.rationale: It challenges the claimed consolatory advantage of Christian eschatology.

responseComponents.description: Disputes that Christian afterlife teaching necessarily offers a less bleak picture.

moves.speaker: John Lennox
moves.claim: The cross portrays God as entering human suffering rather than remaining distant from it.
moves.warrant: Lennox interprets God on the cross as God personally becoming part of the problem of human suffering.
moves.inference: Christianity offers a morally relevant divine response to suffering through participation, even before a complete explanation of each tragedy.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This short passage isolates Lennox's first and self-contained cross-based response.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: he has not remained distant from the problem

moves.attributionRationale: Lennox explicitly takes the response after Tooley's turn.
moves.importanceRationale: It is a distinct Christian response to suffering and atonement, though it does not alone explain preventable evil.

burdenContact.rationale: It presents the cross as part of Christianity's account of suffering.

responseComponents.description: Begins Lennox's answer to the claim that Christian salvation and judgment are bleak.

moves.speaker: John Lennox
moves.claim: Moral freedom is an original good that permits love and rebellion, so eliminating every possibility of moral evil would eliminate genuinely free humans.
moves.warrant: Lennox contrasts humans with robots, says love requires the possibility of hate, and uses parenthood to illustrate accepting the risk of rebellion.
moves.inference: The possibility of moral evil can be compatible with divine goodness if coercion would destroy morally significant freedom.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This span isolates Lennox's complete free-will defense and ends before his separate qualification about Holocaust victims and hell.

moves.importanceRationale: It supplies Lennox's principal moral account of freedom and hell.

burdenContact.rationale: It aims to reconcile Christian divine goodness with moral evil and final separation.

responseComponents.description: Offers morally significant freedom as an explanation for the possibility of moral evil.

moves.speaker: John Lennox

moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This contiguous passage preserves Lennox's explicit Holocaust-victim qualification and his complete informed-rejection account, distinct from the preceding free-will defense.

moves.importanceRationale: It states the doctrinal scope of Lennox's answer to Tooley's hell objection.

moves.speaker: Michael Tooley
moves.claim: God could preserve extensive freedom for loving or vicious choices while imposing stronger limits on the horrendous harm agents can inflict.
moves.warrant: Human powers already have limits, and further limits would still leave wide scope for good and evil choices.

moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is Tooley's complete direct answer to the free-will defense, ending before he changes to final judgment.

moves.speaker: Michael Tooley
moves.claim: A final judgment that fixes a person's fate after a limited earthly period is morally inferior to allowing continued time for reflection and change.
moves.warrant: Tooley describes a person dying after rejecting Jesus and then having no further opportunity to revise that choice.
moves.inference: Appeal to free choice does not by itself justify making the consequences of a temporally limited decision final.

moves.importanceRationale: It tests the moral coherence of Lennox's informed-rejection account.

burdenContact.rationale: It raises a Christian-specific moral objection to final judgment.

responseComponents.description: Challenges whether an informed rejection justifies irreversible consequences after death.

moves.speaker: John Lennox
moves.claim: Science and Christianity are not inherently in conflict because scientists can share scientific practice while differing between atheistic and Christian worldviews.
moves.warrant: Lennox contrasts atheist physicist Peter Higgs with Christian physicist William Phillips and notes that historical pioneers practiced science as theists.
moves.inference: Scientific competence does not decide between theism and atheism, so the dispute must be assessed at the worldview level.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This span contains only the compatibility and shared-science argument, ending before Lennox begins the God-of-the-gaps explanation.

moves.importanceRationale: It establishes Lennox's main framework for relating scientific and theistic explanations.

burdenContact.rationale: It blocks a science-versus-God exclusion and permits Christianity to compete at a worldview level.

moves.warrant: Lennox contrasts a jet engine's thermodynamic and engineering explanation with explanation by its maker, after rejecting a God confined to gaps in knowledge.

moves.importanceRationale: It supplies the central inferential bridge for compatibility between science and theistic agency.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that scientific and agent explanations can jointly apply.

moves.speaker: John Lennox

moves.inference: The possibility and reliability of science fit better with an intelligent creator than with an unguided material account.

moves.warrant: He reports conversations with serious-minded doctors who regarded such cases as real while expressly conceding that this was not direct evidence.
moves.inference: There is testimony worth investigating, but Lennox does not present it as conclusive verification.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This brief passage is the entirety of Lennox's qualified response on possession.

But that's anecdotal

moves.importanceRationale: It is a bounded audience reply with limited evidential ambition.

burdenContact.rationale: It preserves a modest testimonial input relevant to supernatural claims while conceding its limits.

moves.speaker: John Lennox
moves.claim: Asking who created God assumes God is created, whereas Christian theism posits God as eternal ultimate reality just as some atheists posit an eternal universe or mass-energy.
moves.warrant: Lennox distinguishes created creators from the uncreated God and observes that both sides commonly terminate explanation in something ultimate.
moves.inference: The regress question does not uniquely disqualify theism; the substantive comparison concerns which proposed ultimate reality explains better.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is Lennox's complete answer to the audience question about God's origin, including the shared ultimate-reality framing.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: God is utterly eternal
we're really asking about ultimate reality
moves.attributionRationale: Lennox announces the question he is answering and speaks uninterrupted.
moves.importanceRationale: It clarifies the terminus of Lennox's explanation and neutralizes a simple regress objection.

burdenContact.rationale: It reframes the comparison around rival ultimate realities rather than a creator regress.

moves.speaker: Michael Tooley
moves.claim: Although either God or the physical universe could be eternal, an account that derives complex things from simpler predecessors is intellectually preferable, other things equal.
moves.warrant: Tooley contrasts an eternal world always containing complex organisms with evolutionary explanation that reduces complexity to simpler origins.
moves.inference: The key issue is not whether ultimate reality can be eternal but whether positing God introduces unexplained complexity.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This is Tooley's complete reply accepting eternal reality and developing the independent simplicity objection.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: It could be God
reduce complexity and go back to simpler and simpler things
moves.attributionRationale: The moderator permits Tooley to comment, and he directly agrees with John before distinguishing his concern.
moves.importanceRationale: It identifies the live explanatory criterion after conceding Lennox's regress point.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that comparative reasonableness turns partly on explanatory simplicity.

responseComponents.description: Concedes eternal ultimate reality but argues that simplicity remains a comparative concern.

moves.speaker: John Lennox
moves.claim: An explanation need not be simpler than what it explains, as an author's more complex mind can explain a book.
moves.warrant: Lennox applies Tooley's simplicity rule to The God Delusion and notes that its source is Richard Dawkins's more complex mind.
moves.inference: God's alleged complexity does not by itself show that God cannot explain a less complex effect.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This span contains only Lennox's direct complexity reply and ends before he begins the distinct semiotic-information argument.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the infinitely more complex mind of Richard Dawkins
the explanation was more complex than the thing I was explaining
moves.attributionRationale: Lennox takes over after Tooley's question and gives a continuous answer.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly answers the claim that a more complex cause cannot explain a less complex effect.

burdenContact.rationale: It blocks complexity alone from disqualifying an intelligent ultimate cause.

responseComponents.description: Rejects a universal rule that explanations must be less complex than what they explain.

moves.speaker: John Lennox
moves.claim: Symbolically meaningful information ordinarily supports an inference to intelligence, and Lennox extends that inference to genomic coding.
moves.warrant: Written words prompt an immediate agency inference; the genome has a four-letter alphabet and codes for proteins.
moves.inference: The semiotic dimension of biological information may point toward intelligent agency rather than chance and necessity alone.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This span isolates the semiotic argument from its opening principle through its genomic application and worldview conclusion.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: you immediately infer an intelligent input
It codes for the proteins
moves.attributionRationale: Lennox continues his clearly owned response without a speaker change.
moves.importanceRationale: It is a distinct positive agency inference rather than merely a reply about complexity.

burdenContact.rationale: It offers biological information as evidence for intelligent agency.

moves.speaker: Michael Tooley

moves.warrant: Tooley analogizes Jesus' sacrifice to caning an innocent student instead of the student who stole an apple.

moves.speaker: Michael Tooley
moves.claim: Contradictory source strands in the Noah story and allegedly unsupported Old Testament miracles count against biblical reliability when it reports miracles, including the resurrection.
moves.warrant: Tooley says source separation yields differing animal counts and cites the flood, firstborn deaths and sun standing still as events he believes evidence rejects.
moves.inference: A cumulative record of unreliable miracle reports weakens confidence in the Bible's testimony to Jesus' resurrection.

unreliability when it deal deals with miracle stories

burdenContact.rationale: It links alleged biblical unreliability to reduced warrant for Christian miracles.

responseComponents.description: Challenges the reliability of the textual basis for the resurrection evidence Lennox invokes.

moves.speaker: John Lennox
moves.claim: Multiple sources do not entail error, and biblical interpretation must recognize metaphor and literary form rather than impose a uniformly literal reading.
moves.warrant: Lennox notes Luke's explicit use of sources, cites scholarly disagreement about Noah, and illustrates genre sensitivity with 'I am the door' and 'flowing with milk and honey.'

moves.speaker: John Lennox
moves.claim: Humans can create local meanings without God, but atheism removes ultimate meaning and threatens the basis for objective value.
moves.warrant: Lennox expressly concedes invented human meanings, then invokes hard atheistic denials of good, evil and justice and asks what nonmaterial standpoint could resist genetic determination.
moves.inference: Christianity better preserves ultimate significance and moral agency even though atheistic lives can contain humanly created purpose.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This full answer preserves Lennox's concession about ordinary meaning and his distinct claim about ultimate meaning and moral value.

moves.importanceRationale: It is a comparative worldview argument about ultimate rather than everyday meaning.

burdenContact.rationale: It claims Christianity better grounds ultimate significance and moral agency.

moves.speaker: Michael Tooley
moves.claim: Secular ethical realism can ground objective value in necessary ethical truths known through rational intuition, potentially more universally than value based on a nonnecessary deity.
moves.warrant: Tooley sketches ethical intuitionism, compares basic moral truths to necessary mathematical truths, and argues that God's existence is not obviously logically necessary.
moves.inference: Objective morality need not depend on God, and a theistic basis may make moral truth less modally universal than a secular necessary-truth account.

a serious objection to a theistic approach to value

moves.importanceRationale: It provides Tooley's developed positive secular moral account rather than relying only on counterexamples.

burdenContact.rationale: It offers an atheism-compatible route to objective morality against a claimed Christian advantage.

responseComponents.description: Supplies a secular account of objective value against the claimed crisis of meaning.

closings.rationale: The substantive comparative-scope portion of Tooley's available closing is selected. Its later book recommendations repeat the call for inquiry without adding a new argument. The recording ends there; the apparently missing Lennox closing is not reconstructed and creates no adverse inference or penalty.

audienceQuestionAnswers.rationale: All major substantive primary-speaker audience-answer themes are represented. The common-descent audience question receives no completed distinct Lennox answer before the moderator moves on, so no answer is invented.

omissions.sourceSpecificRationale: Initial possession skepticism is represented by Tooley's later qualified audience answer. Repeated formulations of evil, morality and worldview conclusions are merged into their smallest complete representative moves.
Moderator framing, timing decisions, audience-line instructions, applause, laughter and speaker biographies are not participant arguments.

Tooley's closing book recommendations and personal reading advice after event 2390 reinforce inquiry but do not independently support atheism; rhetorical illustrations without a distinct inference and audience premises not adopted by a speaker are omitted.

The moderator bundled questions and limited responses. No interrupted or uncompleted response, including Lennox's attempted one-sentence atonement reply, is treated as a completed move or argumentative absence.
A Lennox closing described elsewhere is absent from every located edition. It is neither reconstructed nor used to infer concession, evasion, failure to answer or lack of argument.

speakerAttributionReview.discussionHandoffs: Opening ownership is fixed at Lennox events 0–201 and Tooley events 203–411. Later named handoffs, direct address and first-person commitments establish ownership even where a moderator briefly says 'Sure' or another speaker interjects.
speakerAttributionReview.audienceQuestionBoundaries: Audience questions begin at event 1718; primary-speaker answers begin at event 1774. Audience and moderator premises are context only and excluded from move ownership.
speakerAttributionReview.mixedSpans: Selected substantive words are assigned only to the named participant. Brief moderator or opponent interjections near events 583, 1507 and 1932–1936 do not supply any selected claim or warrant; source boundaries are narrowed where possible without severing a speaker's complete proposition.
speakerAttributionReview.residualUncertainties: No selected move has materially uncertain ownership. Automatic-caption corruptions are avoided in quote-eligible spans and are not treated as participant errors.

selectionBalanceAudit.rationale: Comparative standards contains two pro and four con moves because Tooley separately defines atheism, distinguishes atheism from rejecting Christianity, raises religious diversity, and qualifies the closing comparison class. Ultimate explanation contains three pro and one con move because Lennox separately advances an eternal-reality answer, a complex-cause reply and a genomic-information inference, while Tooley's single simplicity move supplies the live counter. These source-driven asymmetries keep distinct burdens separate.

sections.rationale: A fourth con row is required for religious diversity, atheism's definition, the separate Christianity burden, and the closing comparison-class qualification.
Fourth rows preserve four distinct pro replies (moral grounding, freedom, informed rejection, final justice) and four distinct con objections (evil, consolation, harmful power, finality).
Three pro rows and one con row remain within ordinary capacity; no fourth row is used.
A fourth pro row is required because the transfiguration reading, two-strands account, later generation reply and qualified possession testimony address distinct claims.
A fourth con row is required because atheism's compatibility with value, cumulative doctrinal morality, substitutionary atonement and secular ethical realism are distinct.
